opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the way to understand that result is in terms of what kind of evidence the learner actually needs to arrive at the right generalization. A lot of the sentences people produce, especially in child-directed speech but also in a lot of ordinary text, are short and simple. And simple sentences are often ambiguous with respect to the underlying structure. If every sentence has one clause and one auxiliary, then a rule like "move the first auxiliary to the front" and a rule like "move the auxiliary of the main clause" make exactly the same predictions. The data just doesn't distinguish between the linear hypothesis and the hierarchical one.

When you add more complex sentences, with embedded clauses, relative clauses, long-distance dependencies, agreement across intervening nouns, you're giving the model cases where those hypotheses come apart. So in a sense it isn't surprising that this helps. The model is getting more disambiguating evidence. The more interesting question, I think, is what it tells us about the model's inductive biases. If a model needs a lot of that disambiguating evidence before it lands on the hierarchical generalization, that suggests its prior doesn't favor hierarchical structure very strongly on its own. It's being pushed there by the data rather than being predisposed to it.

And that's where the comparison with children gets interesting. There's a long-standing argument in linguistics, the poverty of the stimulus argument, that children reach hierarchical generalizations even though the critical disambiguating sentences are fairly rare in what they hear. So if our models only get there when we enrich the input with lots of complex sentences, then that's a sign there's a gap between how these models generalize and how people do. It doesn't necessarily mean the human bias has to be innate in some specifically linguistic sense, but it does mean the human learner is bringing something that a standard transformer trained on next-word prediction isn't bringing, at least not at the same data scale.

So I'd read it as a useful diagnostic. It tells us that the structure of the data matters a lot, and it gives us a handle on separating what's coming from the architecture and training objective from what's coming from the statistics of the input. And practically, it also suggests that if we care about data-efficient learning, thinking carefully about the composition of the training data, not just its quantity, is going to be important.

r001.rationale: The response says complex and embedded sentences provide evidence that separates linear from hierarchical rules, and mentions agreement across intervening nouns. It does not clearly identify the specific heuristic of choosing verb number from the most recent word or describe such sentences as counterexamples to it.

r002.rationale: The response notes that children learn hierarchical generalizations despite rare disambiguating sentences in their input, but does not clearly identify learning correct syntactic rules from the natural sentence distribution as the desired standard for language models.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way to read it is that the complexity of the input is doing something closer to what we'd hope, which is pushing the model away from shallow heuristics. If you train on simple sentences, there are a lot of ways to get the right answer that have nothing to do with syntax. You can just track linear order, or the most recent noun, or whatever, and that'll get you most of the way there. The model has no reason to build hierarchical representations because nothing in the data is forcing it to.

When you add sentences with embedded clauses, relative clauses, that kind of thing, the easy heuristics start to fail. Suddenly the noun that's closest to the verb isn't the subject, and if you've been relying on that, you make mistakes. So the model is under pressure to find a representation that actually generalizes, and the one that generalizes is the structural one. In that sense the finding fits a pretty old idea from acquisition, which is that the learner needs the right kind of evidence, not just more of it.

What I find interesting is that it also complicates the usual story about how much data these models need. People point to the fact that children hear maybe a few tens of millions of words and models see billions and say, well, the model is just a worse learner. That's probably partly true. But this suggests part of the gap is about what's in the data rather than how much there is. Child-directed speech is simpler in some ways, but it's not devoid of structure, and the structure that is there might be unusually informative for the learner.

So I'd be careful about two things. One, this doesn't mean the model has acquired syntax in the way a linguist would describe it. It means it's doing better on tests that are sensitive to syntax, which is a weaker claim. And two, I wouldn't want to over-interpret it as the model needing explicit complex input the way a curriculum would provide it. It may just be that complex sentences are diagnostic, and a model that happens to see enough of them early on gets steered onto a better path. Figuring out which of those is true is, I think, the real follow-up.

r001.rationale: The response says complex sentences make nearest-noun heuristics fail and push models toward structural representations, but it does not clearly specify the heuristic of choosing verb number from the most recent word.

r002.rationale: The response favors structural generalization and informative input, but does not identify learning correct syntactic rules from the natural distribution of sentences as the desired standard for language models.

astra-6.text:
I think one interpretation is that more complex sentences give the model a reason to learn syntax. If most of your training examples are simple sentences, you can do pretty well using a shortcut like agreeing with the most recent noun. In “The key is on the table,” that works. But in “The key to the cabinets is on the table,” the most recent noun would lead you to the wrong prediction. You need to identify which noun is actually the subject.

So complexity can be informative: it can distinguish a structural generalization from a superficial one. I’d be cautious, though, about concluding from improved performance alone that the model has learned syntax in the sense we intend. We’d want to test whether it generalizes to new structures, where other shortcuts won’t work.

r001.rationale: The response explains that complex sentences can defeat the most-recent-noun shortcut, prompting the model to identify the actual subject.

r002.rationale: The response calls for testing generalization to new structures, but does not identify learning correct syntactic rules from the natural distribution of sentences as the desired standard.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the interesting point is that more complex sentences can actually give you more information about the structure of the language. If all you see are very simple sentences, a superficial strategy might work just as well as a genuinely syntactic one. Once you introduce more complex sentences, those strategies start to make different predictions, and the model has an opportunity to learn which generalization is right.

So I would interpret that as evidence that the training distribution matters, not just the amount of data. But I’d be cautious about jumping from improved performance to the conclusion that the model has learned syntax in the same way that humans do. You still want to test whether that knowledge generalizes to new structures, rather than just to sentences that resemble the training examples.

r001.rationale: The response says complex sentences distinguish superficial from syntactic strategies, but does not identify the specific heuristic of choosing verb number from the most recent word or describe complex sentences as counterexamples to it.

r002.rationale: It says the training distribution matters and recommends testing generalization, but does not state that learning correct syntactic rules from the natural sentence distribution is the desired standard.
